attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post, in his own voice.

semantics.note: He states as fact that AI has no ROI. The language is firm and unhedged, so this is a present-tense observation. The context points to LLMs and generative AI.

contract.note: The plain reading (AI spending yields no measurable returns) is the ordinary reading of an absolute claim. The Jan 2025 to post-date window is reasonable. Treating self-reported surveys as weaker evidence is fair to him.

evidence.note: Wharton/GBK survey published Oct 2025, inside the period. Three in four leaders report positive gen-AI returns, and most formally measure ROI. It is self-reported.
Bain survey published June 1, 2026, before the post. It finds a meaningful group of firms realizing their targeted AI savings, which counts against a total absence of ROI.
Same Bain survey: savings widely fell short of targets. This partly supports him, though savings below target are not zero return.
Fortune reporting PwC data (Feb 2026): 56% of firms get nothing from AI yet. This supports him for a majority of firms, not all.
A JPMorgan CEO statement (company disclosure) of roughly $2B benefit for $2B cost. It covers AI broadly and implies about break-even, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The claim is absolute: AI has no ROI. Two independent surveys from inside the period (Wharton, Bain) document positive or realized returns for a meaningful share of firms. That meets the contradiction condition, even with self-reporting discounted. The PwC figure and Bain's shortfall data support a weaker version (most firms lack returns), not the universal one.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: An impossibility claim (nobody can measure AI ROI or standardize per-task cost) with a stated cause (hallucination, harness sprawl). The causal label is correct.

contract.note: The contract rightly notes that he gives no test for what counts as real ROI measurement, and that the causal clause cannot be isolated with public evidence. Treating the claim as untestable is fair.

evidence.note: Available 2026-10-29, after the 2026-10-28 evaluation date, so it cannot be used. In any case it is one vendor's own per-task cost figure, not a cross-harness standard.

reviews.rationale: The claim joins an undefined impossibility ('can't actually measure') with a cause that public evidence cannot isolate. With no accepted test for a valid ROI or standard cost measurement, and no way to attribute the gap to hallucination or harness sprawl, it cannot be scored. The only evidence item is also dated after the evaluation date.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A universal present-tense claim ('every single user of every single' service). The normalization keeps both the universal scope and both halves of the claim.

contract.note: Reading 'subsidized' against actual serving cost fits his contrast with 'the actual cost of AI'. That is ordinary and not stretched. The test that the universal fails if one major service's subscribers cover their serving cost is fair. Choosing H1 2026 is reasonable.

evidence.note: Tom's Hardware item available 2026-10-29, after the evaluation date. It cannot be used.
Same post-cutoff article (available 2026-10-29). It cannot be used.

Summary of the S-1, available 2026-10-27. H1 2026 subscription revenue was $3.2B, and it also reports cost of revenue of $2.4B for all paying customers. Subscriber serving cost is therefore below subscriber revenue in aggregate. These are company-reported figures.

reviews.rationale: Using only pre-cutoff e3: Anthropic's reported H1 2026 cost of serving all paying customers (~$2.4B) is below its subscription revenue alone (~$3.2B). Subscribers as a group paid more than their serving cost, so not every subscriber was subsidized, and the universal claim fails. Caveat: some serving compute may be booked outside cost of revenue.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Won't do it' is an unhedged forecast. In context 'it' means making AI cheaper. No deadline is stated.

contract.note: The cost-not-price reading and the requirement to attribute a cost fall to a named chip are fair. 'Overall cost' should mean the cost of providing comparable work, not total industry spend. The outcome here does not turn on that.

evidence.note: eWeek, June 2026: DeepSeek V4 set off API price cuts. These are price signals, not provider cost evidence, so they do not meet the early-resolution rule.
Available 2026-10-29, after the evaluation date, so it cannot be used. It would only show that compute is not split by chip.

reviews.rationale: This is an open-ended 'won't' forecast with no deadline. Under the contract only early contradiction is possible: a filing or measurement showing a lasting fall in serving cost, attributed to a named chip or to DeepSeek. The usable evidence shows only price cuts, so the forecast stays unresolved.
